content: This review updates the original Cochrane review from 2008, focusing on psychosocial interventions for recurrent abdominal pain (RAP) in children. RAP affects 4% to 25% of school-aged children, often interfering with daily activities. In most cases, no organic cause for the pain is identified through physical examination or diagnostic testing. While many children are managed with reassurance and simple measures, various psychosocial interventions, particularly those with cognitive and behavioral components, have been proposed as treatment options. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of psychosocial interventions in reducing pain in school-aged children with RAP. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing psychosocial therapies to usual care, active control, or wait-list control in children and adolescents aged 5 to 18 years with RAP or functional gastrointestinal disorders as defined by the Rome III criteria. The search for relevant studies was conducted in June 2016 across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, as well as trial registries and reference lists of identified studies. Standard Cochrane methodological procedures were used for study selection, risk of bias assessment, and data extraction. The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Eighteen RCTs, reported in 26 papers, were included in the review, involving 928 children and adolescents aged 6 to 18 years. The interventions were categorized into four types: cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), hypnotherapy (including guided imagery), yoga, and written self-disclosure. The studies were conducted in the USA, Australia, Canada, the Netherlands, Germany, and Brazil. Most studies were small and short-term, with only two studies including more than 100 participants and only five studies having follow-up assessments beyond six months. The overall quality of evidence was rated as low to very low due to small sample sizes and risks of performance and detection bias. For CBT, there was evidence of treatment success immediately after the intervention (odds ratio [OR] 5.67, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.18 to 27.32; 4 studies; 175 children; very low-quality evidence). However, there was no evidence of treatment success at medium-term follow-up (OR 3.08, 95% CI 0.93 to 10.16; 3 studies; 139 children; low-quality evidence) or long-term follow-up (OR 1.29, 95% CI 0.50 to 3.33; 2 studies; 120 children; low-quality evidence). There was also no evidence of an effect on pain intensity scores immediately after the intervention (standardized mean difference [SMD] -0.33, 95% CI -0.74 to 0.08; 7 studies; 405 children; low-quality evidence) or at medium-term follow-up (SMD -0.32, 95% CI -0.85 to 0.20; 4 studies; 301 children; low-quality evidence). For hypnotherapy, including guided imagery, there was evidence of greater treatment success immediately after the intervention (OR 6.78, 95% CI 2.41 to 19.07; 4 studies; 146 children; low-quality evidence). Hypnotherapy also showed reductions in pain intensity (SMD -1.01, 95% CI -1.41 to -0.61; 4 studies; 146 children; low-quality evidence) and pain frequency (SMD -1.28, 95% CI -1.84 to -0.72; 4 studies; 146 children; low-quality evidence). One study reported long-term benefits of hypnotherapy, with 68% of participants reporting treatment success compared to 20% in the control group after five years (P = 0.005). For yoga therapy, there was no evidence of effectiveness in reducing pain intensity immediately after the intervention (SMD -0.31, 95% CI -0.67 to 0.05; 3 studies; 122 children; low-quality evidence). A single study on written self-disclosure therapy found no benefit for pain reduction. There was no evidence of an effect from any intervention on secondary outcomes, including school performance, social or psychological functioning, and quality of daily life. No adverse effects were reported for any of the interventions. In conclusion, the available data suggest that CBT and hypnotherapy may have short-term benefits in reducing pain in children and adolescents with RAP. However, there is no evidence supporting the effectiveness of yoga therapy or written self-disclosure therapy. The quality of evidence is low to very low, and further high-quality, long-term studies are needed to confirm these findings. Future research should aim to identify the active components of these interventions, determine whether benefits are sustained over time, and use active control groups to minimize bias.
